new_statements.quote: Die Betonung wird in der Transkription eines Mundartwortes, in Zweifelsfällen auch bei Fremdwörtern, die im Text aufscheinen, durch das schräge Akzentzeichen über dem betonten Vokal angezeigt. Angesichts der im Deutschen sowie auch im Englischen fast absolut geltenden Erstsilben-Betonung erübrigt sich das Akzentzeichen bei den meisten Wörtern. Die Betonung ist auch dann nicht eigens vermerkt, wenn das Mundartwort, im Einklang mit dem hochdeutschen Sprachgebrauch, als erste Silbe eine untrennbare Vorsilbe aufweist, wonach der Ton dann auf die zweite Silbe fällt. Demnach sind Wörter wie z.B. das Subst /gabrilix/ 'Gebrüll' oder das Adj /gaeweniklix/ 'gewöhnlich' oder das Verb /ferfups/ 'verstopfen' [...] auf der zweiten Silbe betont.
new_statements.translation: In the transcription of a dialect word, and in doubtful cases also for foreign words appearing in the text, stress is indicated by the acute accent mark over the stressed vowel. Given the first-syllable stress that holds almost absolutely in German as well as in English, the accent mark is unnecessary for most words. Stress is also not specially noted when the dialect word, in accordance with High German usage, has an inseparable prefix as its first syllable, in which case the stress falls on the second syllable. Accordingly words such as the noun /gabrilix/ 'Gebrüll', the adjective /gaeweniklix/ 'gewöhnlich', the verb /ferfups/ 'verstopfen' [... the participle /gablasn/ 'geblasen', or hybrid formations derived from an English verb such as /gapelat/ 'gepellet'] are stressed on the second syllable.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable (stem-initial) almost without exception, as in German and English; if the first syllable is an unstressed inseparable prefix (ge-/ga-, ver-/fer-, etc., including on English-derived hybrid verbs like ga-pelat), stress falls on the following (stem) syllable; other deviations (mainly foreign words) are marked individually with an acute in the dictionary transcriptions. Scheer 1972 adds that Russian/Ukrainian loans were nativised by retracting the accent to the first syllable (/'hulba/ < hul'bá, /'liŋkela/ < linéjka).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not treated in the 1987 rule; Scheer 1972 (p.~213) notes for /kratsavits/ 'Gurke' primary stress on the first and secondary stress ('Sekundärton') on the third syllable.
new_statements.exceptions: Inseparable-prefix words stressed on the 2nd syllable; foreign words/loans with non-initial stress are marked case by case with an acute (e.g. dictionary entries noting 'Betonung auf der zweiten Silbe des hutt Mw'); English loans like the jam/jelly/marmalade entry show first-syllable stress against 3rd-syllable stress of the Standard German cognate.
new_statements.domain_note: Statement concerns citation forms of dictionary headwords (word level), framed as a transcription convention for the Hutterisch-German-English dictionary; based on Scheer's fieldwork in Dariusleut, Lehrerleut and Schmiedeleut colonies (Alberta, South Dakota, Minnesota, Manitoba).
new_statements.identity_note: Scheer 1987 describes Hutterisch as spoken across Dariusleut, Lehrerleut and Schmiedeleut colonies (Alberta, South Dakota, Minnesota, Manitoba) = glottocode hutt1235 (ISO geh); no separate dialect glottocode. Hoover 1997 (list of works to obtain) describes the Prairieleut variety at Langham, Saskatchewan.
